title: The UK is safe—for now
gist: Andrew Adonis argues the UK union is safe while Andy Burnham is prime minister: nationalist leaders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are cautious and support for constitutional change is shallow, even after Trump's remark about a united Ireland. A Farage-led Reform government's disrespect, especially over the Brexit settlement, could quickly tip it into existential crisis, with Ireland the likeliest flashpoint.

insights.claim: Donald Trump's aside that a united Ireland 'may as well happen now' was met with barely a shrug, with taoiseach Micheál Martin downplaying it most, saying he was 'not into timelines' and backing the Good Friday agreement.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Near-term Irish unification risk is low; Dublin is a stabilising force.
insights.locator: Europe’s leaders have become collectively weary

insights.claim: Europe's leaders have become weary and 'unshocked' by Trump's provocations unless they are backed by actual force.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Markets and politicians are discounting Trump rhetoric; only force moves them.
insights.locator: Europe’s leaders have become collectively weary

insights.claim: Meeting in Cardiff, the nationalist leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland declared 'Westminster's time is coming to an end' but set no date, and Welsh first minister Rhun ap Iorwerth would not commit to an independence referendum.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Rhetoric without timelines means low near-term break-up risk for UK assets.
insights.quote: “Westminster’s time is coming to an end,” they declared in a joint statement.

insights.claim: Andy Burnham has firmly ruled out constitutional referendums in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and Adonis expects no change while Burnham is in power because he is unlikely to stir anti-Westminster animosity.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: UK break-up risk premium should stay low under a Burnham government.
insights.locator: I doubt this situation will change

insights.claim: Nationalist votes in Scotland and Wales largely reflect disillusion with Labour and opposition to Reform UK rather than a passion for independence, while Northern Irish voters prioritise the peace and prosperity of the Good Friday agreement.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Distinguish nationalist party support from referendum risk when pricing UK constitutional risk.
insights.locator: In all three jurisdictions it is important

insights.claim: Polls show barely a third of Welsh voters support independence, Scotland rejected it only 12 years ago, and after 19 lacklustre years in government the SNP is popular only relative to the alternatives.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Low independence momentum; referendum risk is not imminent.

insights.claim: The final Brexit deal defused the Irish unification push by keeping the Irish border open without checks while Northern Ireland effectively stays in the EU single market.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: The Windsor-style settlement is the key stabiliser; any breach reopens unification risk.

insights.claim: A Reform UK victory at the next election could trigger another Brexit-style bout of aggressive, incompetent English nationalism, turning latent nationalism into a potent force through constant acts of disrespect.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: A Reform win is a tail risk for UK constitutional stability and gilt and sterling risk premia.
insights.locator: However, all that could change quickly

insights.claim: With nationalists already governing in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast, a Farage government could send the UK into existential crisis quickly, with Ireland the likeliest flashpoint if it breached the Brexit settlement to please the DUP.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Watch Reform's stance on the Northern Ireland protocol and Windsor arrangements as a key UK-EU risk indicator.

insights.claim: In that scenario a taoiseach could call for an EU-backed unification process with cross-community support in Northern Ireland, leaving a Farage government exposed, especially with a US president saying unification 'may as well happen now'.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: A low-probability, high-impact scenario for UK break-up risk.
